name: Abital
title: David's wife in Hebron and mother of Shephatiah
summary: Abital belonged to the circle of wives that King David married during his seven and a half years as king in Hebron over Judah. She is known as the mother of Shephatiah, David's fifth son according to the order in 2 Samuel. Both in this writing and in 1 Chronicles she is mentioned in the lists of David's wives and their sons. Beyond these two brief references, Abital remains a quiet figure in the biblical narrative, with no information given about her background, family, or later life.

keyEvents.title: Married to David in Hebron
keyEvents.description: Abital became one of David's wives during the period when he reigned as king over Judah in Hebron. She gave birth to her son Shephatiah, who was the fifth of David's sons born in this city.

keyEvents.title: Recorded in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Abital and her son Shephatiah are also recorded in the genealogy in 1 Chronicles, as part of the overview of David's royal family in Hebron.

versions.summary: Abital was one of King David's wives during his reign in Hebron. She bore David a son named Shephatiah, who was David's fifth son. She is mentioned among the wives David took while he reigned over Judah from Hebron.

versions.reason: [minor] The title is precise enough, but could have been slightly more informative by mentioning that she was the mother of Shephatiah, since that is her primary biblical role.; [major] The role 'queen' is misleading. Abigail is not referred to as queen in the Bible. She was one of David's many wives, but there is no indication that she held any formal title of queen. More precise would be 'wife' or 'royal wife'.; [minor] The summary is acceptable, but states that Shephatiah was David's fifth son. According to 2 Sam 3:4, Shephatiah is the fifth son mentioned in the list – this is correct. The summary is essentially accurate.; [minor] The first two events both refer to exactly the same verse (2 Sam 3:4) and overlap thematically. They could have been combined into one event to avoid redundancy, but it is not an error.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. It would have been interesting to include a linguistic note on the meaning of the name Abital, as well as a historical note about David's Hebron period.

versions.summary: Abital was one of King David's wives during his reign in Hebron, where he ruled over Judah for seven and a half years. She bore David a son named Shephatiah, who was David's fifth son born in Hebron. Abital is mentioned both in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles among David's wives, but beyond this, the Bible gives no further information about her.

footnotes.text: The name Abital (Hebrew: אֲבִיטָל, 'Avital') likely means 'my father is dew' or 'dew-father'. In Semitic naming tradition, 'father' (אָב, 'av') can refer to God, while 'dew' (טַל, 'tal') symbolizes blessing, freshness, and life-giving power (cf. Ps 133:3; Hos 14:6). The name can thus be understood as a theological expression of divine care.

David reigned in Hebron over the tribe of Judah for seven and a half years (c. 1010–1003 BC) before he captured Jerusalem and became king over all Israel. During this period, he took several wives, which was common among kings in the ancient Near East to strengthen political alliances and secure succession.

The list of David's sons born in Hebron (2 Sam 3:2–5) reflects a royal tradition known throughout the ancient Near East, where princely sons were carefully recorded to document succession and dynastic legitimacy. A parallel list is found in 1 Chron 3:1–4.

Hebron was one of the oldest and most important cities in the Judean highlands. Archaeological excavations at Tel Hebron (Tell er-Rumeide) have uncovered settlement layers from the Bronze Age and Iron Age, confirming the city's significance during the period when David, according to the biblical text, reigned there.

Shephatiah, Abital's son, is David's fifth son according to the order in 2 Sam 3:4. Despite his position in the succession, he played no known political role in the later struggles for the throne among David's sons, such as Absalom and Adonijah. This may indicate that his mother's family had limited political influence.
